thread:
sanjay: Quick RFC follow-up — I sketched a smaller opt-in controller surface that only carries intent for short-lived surge lanes. Wanted to capture tradeoffs before we freeze the API.

maria: 👍 share the sketch pls. the last proposal felt too heavy weight for tenants who only need occasional bursts.

sanjay: Pasted below. Key idea: controller emits 'surge-intent' objects (TTL short, e.g. 2m) with desired burst width + max cost band. Operator is authoritative for capacity enforcement and billing but subscribes to intents.

jamie: Hmm. How do we avoid oscillation when intents pile up? If many tenants emit 2m intents at the same time, operator could accept then quickly reject.

sanjay: We add a queued smoothing stage in the operator and a small admission window. Operator maintains a token budget per pool and converts intents into provisional reservations. If provisional + committed > safety headroom -> apply backoff to the oldest provisional intents.

srinivas: Can you show the contract shape? snippet would help for SDK/product.

sanjay: Sure: 
```
intent = {
  tenant_id: string,
  burst_tokens: int,
  max_cost_band: string,
  ttl_seconds: int,
  affinity_hint: [zone],
}
```
Operator returns status: ACCEPTED / QUEUED / REJECTED + estimated wait.

maria: Who owns 'estimated wait'? operator obviously, but controller should surface quick fallback suggestions (like fallback model variant). That matters for UX.

anna: From product POV we need a deterministic SLA mapping. If controller only emits intent and operator can silently throttle, customers will be confused. Need explicit SLA levels: best-effort, burst-guaranteed (requires reservation), and reserved.

jamie: Agreed. So controller should allow tenants to mark priority level on intents and attach a commit token if they want stronger guarantees (and cost implications). commit_token = optional opaque id that operator uses to charge.

orch-bot: new message recorded: policy-change:surge-operator-adapter v0.3 deployed to staging.

srinivas: Implementation nit: provisional reservations need a decay callback so long-living queued intents don't hog admission. I suggest exponential decay + penalty multiplier after n retries.

sanjay: Good point. Also debating whether the controller should perform predictive prewarm (based on telemetry) or leave that to the operator. Predictive prewarm may require access to global telemetry and could leak cross-tenant signals.

maria: If predictive prewarm lives in controller it can be tenant-scoped and run locally per deployment, but we lose cluster-level efficiency. Operator-level predictive prewarm can coalesce similar patterns but needs more infra + privacy controls.

anna: Product preference: conservative start — keep predictive prewarm as opt-in operator feature with clear privacy docs. Controller can emit richer signals (non-identifying) if tenant opts in.

jamie: Another tradeoff: a single admission API vs. two-step (intent then allocate). Single-call is simpler but couples controller and operator. Two-step is more robust for retries and for providing wait estimates.

srinivas: Two-step also lets us stream status updates to caller (useful for interactive flows). I vote two-step with an async status endpoint.

sanjay: plan: update RFC with: 1) intent object shape above, 2) three SLA levels, 3) two-step flow (intent -> provisional -> commit), 4) operator-side decay/backoff heuristics, 5) predictive prewarm opt-in operator feature. I'll ping infra owners for privacy review.

maria: love it. can we add a tiny sample SDK pseudocode in the RFC showing typical client flow and fallback path?

sanjay: yes — will add. Example: 
```python
# optimistic burst use
intent_id = controller.create_intent(burst_tokens=200, ttl=120)
status = operator.poll_intent(intent_id)
if status == 'ACCEPTED': call_model()
else: call_fallback_model()
```

anna: timeline? customers asked for a preview next week for the sales demos.
